A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have been able to show that aphasia is not a unitary disorder, that the symptoms of aphasia can be explained by the disturbance of a number of separate functions, and that these functions are not localizable in the brain in any simple way.

we have succeeded in establishing a connection between aphasic symptoms and the localization of the lesions, which has hitherto been lacking, and in doing so have made use of the most recent discoveries of the brain sciences and of the most recent views of the nature of aphasia.
the aphasic disturbances of speech are due not to lesions of particular areas but to lesions of particular functional processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a computer, but a network of networks, and that the networks are not static, but dynamic, with the potential to change in response to experience.
the brain is not a passive substrate for the mind.
there is no single, simple, and straightforward relationship between brain structure and function.
